blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: No guide of yours covers this subject, so this part was written for the site, as of October 2026. Frontend libraries change quickly: check the official documentation before relying on a detail.

Before React, code changed the page directly: find this element, update its text, add a class. As screens grew, keeping everything in step became the hard part. React changes the question. You describe **what the screen should look like for the current data**, and React works out how to update the page.

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[State changes] --> B[React calls your component]
  B --> C[New description of the UI]
  C --> D[React compares it with the previous one]
  D --> E[Only the differences are applied to the DOM]
  E --> F[User acts]
  F --> A
blocks.title: UI as a function of state

blocks.text: ### Setting up

blocks.code:
npm create vite@latest shop -- --template react-ts
cd shop
npm install
npm run dev
blocks.title: Create a project with Vite

blocks.text:
Vite serves your code during development and bundles it for production. Think of `package.json` as your `pom.xml`, `npm` as Maven, and `node_modules` as a local `.m2`. Commit `package-lock.json`, so that every machine installs the same versions.

| Java world | Frontend world |
|---|---|
| Maven or Gradle | npm, pnpm |
| `pom.xml` | `package.json` |
| Compiler plus jar | Vite bundling |
| JUnit | Vitest |
| Checkstyle | ESLint, Prettier |

### Components and JSX

A component is a function that returns a description of UI.

blocks.title: Your first component

blocks.text:
JSX isn't HTML. It compiles to function calls, so: | HTML | JSX | Why | |---|---|---| | `class` | `className` | `class` is a keyword | | `for` | `htmlFor` | `for` is a keyword | | `onclick="..."` | `onClick={fn}` | Pass a function, not text | | `style="color:red"` | `style={{ color: 'red' }}` | An object | | `
` | `
` | Every tag must close | A component must start with a capital letter, and return one parent element. Use a fragment, `<>...`, to group without an extra DOM node.
`{count && <Badge />}` shows a literal `0` when count is 0, because `0` is what `&&` returns, and React renders numbers. Write `{count > 0 && <Badge />}`.
blocks.title: The 0 trap

blocks.text:
### Props

Props are a component's parameters. They flow **down** from parent to child, and are read-only. To let a child affect a parent, pass a function.

blocks.title: Passing data down and events up

blocks.text:
### Composition

The special `children` prop lets you build wrappers, and React prefers this to inheritance. You'll almost never write `extends` for components.

blocks.title: Composition
Key points
blocks.text:
- Describe the UI for the current data
- A component is a function
- JSX compiles to calls, not HTML
- Data flows down, and events flow up

### State

Regular variables reset on each render, and changing them doesn't update the screen. State survives renders, and changing it schedules a new render.

blocks.title: A counter

blocks.text:
### State is a snapshot

This surprises nearly everyone at first. During one render, `count` is a fixed value, and setting state doesn't change it until the next render.

blocks.title: Why this adds only 1

blocks.text:
Use the updater form whenever the new value depends on the old one. React also batches several updates in one event into a single render.

### Never mutate state

React detects change by comparing references with `Object.is`. A mutated object is still the same reference, so nothing happens.

blocks.title: Always make a new value

blocks.text:
Deep updates get verbose. Keep state flat, or use a helper such as Immer.

### What makes a component render?

1. Its own state changes.
2. Its parent renders.
3. A context it reads changes.

Note the second: **by default, when a parent renders, all its children render too**, even if props are unchanged. A render isn't a DOM update: React calls the function and compares, and then often changes nothing.

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Trigger: state change] --> B[Render: call components, build a tree]
  B --> C[Reconcile: compare with the previous tree]
  C --> D[Commit: apply changes to the DOM]
  D --> E[Effects run]
blocks.title: Render and commit

blocks.text:
### Derived data isn't state

If you can calculate it from existing state or props, then don't store it.

blocks.title: Calculate during render

blocks.text:
### Where to put state: lifting up

When two components need the same data, move the state to their closest common parent, and pass it down.

blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  P[Parent: owns selectedId] -->|selectedId| A[List]
  P -->|selectedId| B[Details]
  A -->|onSelect| P
blocks.title: Lifting state up

blocks.text: **"Why doesn't my state update right away?"** State is a snapshot for each render. A setter schedules a new render, and the current variable keeps its value. Use the updater form for repeated changes, and `useEffect` only if you must react after the commit.
blocks.title: Interview answer
Key points
blocks.text:
- State is a snapshot per render
- Use updaters when building on the old value
- Never mutate state
- Don't store what can be calculated
### Rendering lists

blocks.title: Map to elements

blocks.text:
### Keys matter

A key tells React which item is which between renders. It must be stable and unique among siblings.

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A["Before: [0: Asha, 1: Bala]"] --> B["Insert Dev at top"]
  B --> C["After: [0: Dev, 1: Asha, 2: Bala]"]
  C --> D["React thinks item 0 changed from Asha to Dev, and keeps item 0's input text and state"]
blocks.title: Index keys go wrong when items change position

blocks.text: With index keys, state inside a row stays at the position rather than with the data, so a half-typed input can appear on the wrong person's row. Use a real ID.
Avoid `key={Math.random()}`, which remounts every row on every render, destroying state and speed. Index keys are acceptable only for static lists that never reorder.
blocks.title: Key mistakes

blocks.text:
Keys have another use: changing a key tells React to throw away and recreate a component. `<EditForm key={user.id} user={user} />` resets the form's state whenever the user changes, with no effect needed.

### State belongs to a position

React keeps state tied to a component's place in the tree.

blocks.title: Same position, same state

blocks.text:
Never declare a component inside another component. A new function is created on each render, so React sees a new type, and destroys all state below it. It's a frequent cause of "my input loses focus on every keystroke".

### Conditional rendering

blocks.code:
if (isLoading) return <Spinner />;               // an early return

{error ? <ErrorBox message={error} /> : <Results />}   // either-or

{isAdmin && <AdminPanel />}                      // show or nothing
blocks.title: Common patterns

blocks.text: ### Handling events

blocks.code:
<button onClick={save}>Save</button>             // right
<button onClick={save()}>Save</button>           // wrong: runs during render
<button onClick={() => remove(order.id)}>Delete</button>  // with an argument
blocks.title: Passing a function, not calling it

blocks.text:
### Controlled inputs

In React, the state usually owns the input's value.

blocks.title: A controlled input

blocks.text: Each keystroke updates state, which renders the input with its new value. It also means you can validate or transform as people type. Part 7 covers forms in depth.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Use stable IDs as keys
- State belongs to a position in the tree
- Don't define components inside components
- Pass functions, don't call them

### Think in components

1. Draw boxes around the screen's parts.
2. Build a static version from props.
3. Find the minimal state.
4. Decide who owns each piece of state.
5. Add events that change it.

### Project layout

blocks.code:
src/
  features/
    orders/
      OrderList.tsx
      OrderDetails.tsx
      useOrders.ts
      orders.api.ts
      orders.test.tsx
    auth/
  components/        shared UI: Button, Modal
  lib/               API client, utilities
  App.tsx
  main.tsx
blocks.title: Organise by feature

blocks.text:
Grouping by feature keeps related code together, and it's what you do in Spring packages too. This site is organised this way.

### Separate data from display

blocks.title: Container and presentational parts

blocks.text:
### Handling errors

An error thrown during render would unmount the whole app, unless an **error boundary** catches it. These are one of the rare remaining uses of class components, or use the `react-error-boundary` library.

blocks.code:
This section couldn't load.

}>
blocks.title: An error boundary around a risky part

blocks.text:
They catch render errors, but not errors in event handlers or async code. Handle those with `try` and `catch`, or through your data library.

### Lazy loading and Suspense

blocks.code:
const Reports = lazy(() => import('./features/reports/Reports'));

<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
  <Reports />
</Suspense>
blocks.title: Load a heavy page only when needed

blocks.text:
### Component rules of thumb

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| One job per component | Easier to test and reuse |
| Under about 200 lines | Past that, it usually does too much |
| Avoid passing props through many layers | Use composition or context |
| Keep components pure | Same props and state give the same output |
| Hooks at the top level | The rules of hooks require it |

**Pure** matters: rendering shouldn't change anything outside itself. React's Strict Mode calls components twice in development to expose violations, which is why you may see effects and logs run twice.

### What's new in React 19

| Feature | Use |
|---|---|
| `ref` as a normal prop | No more `forwardRef` in most cases |
| Actions and `useActionState` | Form submission state |
| `useOptimistic` | Show success immediately |
| `use()` | Read a promise or context in render |
| React Compiler | Automatic memoisation at build time |
| `<title>` and `<meta>` in components | Document metadata |

Your hooks and forms parts cover the main ones. This site runs on React 19.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Group code by feature
- Separate data loading from display
- Error boundaries catch render errors
- Keep components pure

Let's apply "think in components" from start to finish on a small screen: a product list with search, an in-stock filter, and an add-to-cart button.

### Step 1: draw the boxes

blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A[ProductPage: owns query, inStockOnly and cart] --> B[SearchBar]
  A --> C[ProductList]
  A --> D[CartSummary]
  C --> E[ProductRow]
blocks.title: The component tree

blocks.text:
### Step 2: find the minimal state

Go through each piece of data, and ask three questions.

| Data | Changes over time? | Comes from props? | Calculable? | State? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All products | No | Yes, from a parent or the API | | No |
| Search text | Yes | No | No | **Yes** |
| In-stock checkbox | Yes | No | No | **Yes** |
| Filtered list | Yes | | Yes, from the above | No |
| Cart items | Yes | No | No | **Yes** |
| Cart total | Yes | | Yes, from the cart | No |

So there are three pieces of state, and everything else is calculated during render.

### Step 3: the code

blocks.title: The complete feature

blocks.text:
### Why it's built this way

- **`visible` and `total` aren't state,** so they can't disagree with their sources.
- **`SearchBar` holds no state.** Its parent owns it, so that the list can use it too.
- **`onAdd` uses an updater,** so rapid clicks all count.
- **A `form` with a `role`,** and real labels, means that the screen is accessible, and tests can find everything by role.
- **Empty state is handled,** which is often forgotten.

### What would change in a real app

| This example | Production |
|---|---|
| Products as a prop | TanStack Query |
| `query` in state | URL search params, so that links are shareable |
| Cart in state | Stored per user, on the server |
| Filter on every key | Fine for hundreds; debounce and paginate on the server for thousands |
| `price` as a number | Integer paise, or a string from the API |

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Ask three questions to find state
- Calculate the rest during render
- Parents own shared state
- Always handle the empty state

Reading real codebases means recognising these patterns.

### Compound components

Related components share state implicitly, giving a flexible API. Tabs are the classic example.

blocks.title: Tabs as compound components

blocks.text:
A full ARIA tabs pattern also needs arrow-key navigation, which tested libraries such as Radix provide.

### Controlled or uncontrolled components

Good reusable components can support both modes.

blocks.title: A component that works either way

blocks.text:
### Render props and slots

Pass a function as a prop, so that a component controls logic while the caller controls display. Hooks replaced many uses, but they're still common in lists, tables and virtualisers.

blocks.code:
<Layout
  header={<Header />}
  sidebar={<Nav />}
>
  <Content />
</Layout>
blocks.title: Slots are simply props holding elements

blocks.text:
### Portals

Render to another part of the DOM, escaping `overflow: hidden` and stacking contexts. Events still bubble through the **React** tree.

blocks.title: A modal through a portal

blocks.text:
### Higher-order components

A function that takes a component and returns another, such as `withAuth(Page)`. You'll see them in older code, but custom hooks usually replace them today.

### Which pattern when?

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Share logic | Custom hook |
| Share layout | `children` and slots |
| Related parts sharing state | Compound components |
| Customise rendering of items | Render prop |
| Escape parent's overflow | Portal |

Patterns are tools rather than goals. Reach for the simplest thing, and only add a pattern when plain props become awkward.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Compound components share state implicitly
- Reusable components can be controlled or not
- Portals escape overflow, not the React tree
- Hooks replaced most HOCs
### The main options, in code

blocks.title: CSS Modules: scoped by default
Tailwind: utilities in the markup

blocks.text: Tailwind scans your files for complete class strings. `bg-${color}-500` won't work, as that class never appears anywhere. Use a lookup: `{ red: 'bg-red-500', green: 'bg-green-500' }[color]`.
blocks.title: Tailwind needs whole class names

blocks.text: ### Reusable variants

blocks.title: A button with typed variants

blocks.text:
Extending `ComponentProps<'button'>` means `type`, `disabled` and `onClick` all work and are typed, without declaring each.

### Component libraries

| Library | Character |
|---|---|
| shadcn/ui | Copy components into your repo, built on Radix and Tailwind |
| Radix, React Aria | Unstyled and accessible; you add looks |
| Material UI | Complete and styled; common in enterprises |
| Ant Design | Rich data components; common for admin panels |

For an internal tool with tables and forms, a complete library saves weeks. Don't hand-build dialogs, date pickers and comboboxes, because accessible versions are harder than they look.

### Design tokens

Keep colours, spacing and radii as named tokens, in CSS variables or a Tailwind theme, rather than hard-coded values. This makes dark mode and rebranding easy. This site defines its tokens in `src/index.css`.

### Icons and images in React

Use an icon library such as Lucide, which allows tree shaking. Importing a whole icon font or set increases your bundle. Decorative icons need `aria-hidden`, and icon-only buttons need a label.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- CSS Modules scope styles
- Tailwind needs complete class names
- Use libraries for complex widgets
- Name your design values
#### The idea behind React

items.question: Why does {items.length && <List />} sometimes show 0?
items.answer: `&&` returns 0 when the length is 0, and React renders that number. Use `items.length > 0 &&`.

items.question: How does a child tell its parent something?
items.answer: The parent passes a function as a prop, and the child calls it.

items.question: Why doesn't React use inheritance for sharing component behaviour?
items.answer: Composition through props and children is more flexible, and custom hooks share logic.

blocks.text: #### State and how rendering works

items.question: Three setCount(count + 1) calls in one handler. What happens?
items.answer: It increases by 1, since each uses the same snapshot. Use `setCount(c => c + 1)`.

items.question: Why doesn't mutating an array in state update the screen?
items.answer: React compares references. It's the same array, so no change is detected.

items.question: Parent state changes, but a child's props don't. Does the child render?
items.answer: Yes, by default. A render doesn't necessarily change the DOM.

blocks.text: #### Lists, keys and conditional rendering

items.question: An input loses focus on every keystroke. What's a common cause?
items.answer: The component is defined inside another, so each render makes a new type and remounts. Or the key changes each render.

items.question: How can you reset a form's state when the selected user changes?
items.answer: Give it `key={user.id}`, so that React creates a fresh instance.

items.question: What's wrong with onClick={save()}?
items.answer: It calls `save` during render. Pass `save`, or an arrow function.

blocks.text: #### Structuring a React application

items.question: Why might a console log appear twice in development?
items.answer: Strict Mode renders twice, to expose impure code. It doesn't do this in production.

items.question: Does an error boundary catch an error from an onClick handler?
items.answer: No. It catches render errors. Use try and catch in handlers.

items.question: Why separate OrdersPage and OrderTable?
items.answer: The table takes only props, which makes it easy to test and reuse, while the page handles data states.

blocks.text: #### Worked example: a product catalogue

items.question: Why isn't the filtered list stored in state?
items.answer: It can be calculated from products, query and the checkbox. Storing it adds a chance for them to disagree.

items.question: Why does SearchBar receive query as a prop rather than own it?
items.answer: The list needs it too, so the state lives in their common parent.

blocks.text: #### Component patterns

items.question: A dropdown inside an overflow: hidden parent gets cut off. What helps?
items.answer: A portal, rendering it at the document body, positioned over the trigger.

items.question: What's the difference between controlled and uncontrolled?
items.answer: In controlled, the parent owns the value through props. In uncontrolled, the component keeps its own state.

items.question: A click inside a portal: does it bubble to the React parent?
items.answer: Yes. Events follow the React tree, even though the DOM node is elsewhere.

blocks.text: #### Styling in React

items.question: Why doesn't `bg-${color}-500` work with Tailwind?
items.answer: Tailwind finds class names by scanning source text, and that complete string never appears.

items.question: Why extend ComponentProps<'button'> in a Button?
items.answer: All native button props are accepted and typed, with no need to redeclare them.
